title: Pydantic is STILL all you need: Jason Liu

primary.label: Prompting & LLM Programming
primary.rationale: Selected by Jev (System One, jev-1.13.0) from the 17-category taxonomy using the talk's summary, takeaways, concepts and technologies (confidence 97%).

domains.label: General Purpose
domains.rationale: The talk's central focus is structured outputs and LLM-as-program patterns using Pydantic and the Instructor library, fitting the structured generation and compiler-style LLM programming criteria. Structured output patterns are cross-domain, demonstrated across RAG, classification, data extraction, and vision, while the Instructor library is a developer tool for software builders. Content centers on development patterns and tooling for building LLM applications with structured outputs. Requires familiarity with Python, Pydantic, LLM function calling, and API concepts per the stated prerequisites. Recorded conference presentation at the AI Engineer World's Fair. All cited evidence anchors are graded as said_in_transcript, sourced directly from the transcript.

summary: Jason Liu returns to the AI Engineer World's Fair a year after his popular 'Pydantic is all you need' talk to reinforce that structured outputs remain the foundational approach for working with LLMs. He argues that if an intern returned an API that output a string requiring manual JSON parsing, they'd be fired—yet developers accept this from LLMs. Without schemas, you lose compatibility, composability, and reliability. The Instructor library has reached 1.0, launching in Python, TypeScript, Ruby, Go, Elixir, and Rust, described as the ~600 lines of code you don't want to write yourself. The API design is stable: one noun (the client) and three verbs (create, create with iterable, create with partial), with everything else revolving around response models, validators, and the messages array. Jason demonstrates field-level and model-level validators. Field validators can enforce formatting with error messages fed back to the LLM for self-correction. Model validators can check cross-field constraints, like verifying receipt line items sum to the total cost. For RAG, structured outputs enable generating follow-up questions, validating URLs, and building sophisticated search with multiple indices. A search model can define query, date ranges, limits, and source selection, allowing parallel queries. For data extraction, simple Literal types create classifiers, and chain-of-thought improves accuracy by ~15%. Jason also shows advanced PEP type annotations to extract tables from images, with custom validators and serializers enabling IDE autocomplete for data frame methods. He shares key year-one learnings: one retry is usually enough for OpenAI and Anthropic models, well-written error messages are essential for both human and LLM readability, and new faster models make latency costs acceptable. He notes 4-5% failure rates in complex validations, reducible to zero through fine-tuning on function calling, even for simple models like Mistral or GPT-3.5. He argues structured outputs are here to stay across vision, RAG, and agents, with enterprise RAG moving toward report generation for decision-making and agents toward generating workflows and DAGs for execution engines rather than react loops. Prompting and response models are implementation details; the type system is what matters. The overarching theme: there are no new abstractions—just reducing LLMs back to classical programming with types, turning generative AI into generating data structures, making software 3.0 backward compatible with existing software.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

sections.title: Introduction and Problem Statement
sections.summary: Jason revisits his popular talk from last year, reasserting that Pydantic is still all you need. He frames the problem: developers accept unstructured string outputs from LLMs that they'd never accept from a human intern, losing compatibility, composability, and reliability. The solution is structured outputs with schemas, nested models, and validators.

sections.title: Instructor Library and API Design
sections.summary: Jason covers what's new: Instructor 1.0 released across six languages with 40% MoM growth in Python. The API is stable with one noun (client) and three verbs (create, create with iterable, create with partial). Response models, validators, and messages arrays are the core abstractions. The API supports OpenAI, Anthropic, Cohere, Gemini, Groq, Ollama, and llama.cpp.

sections.title: Validators and Retry Logic
sections.summary: Jason demonstrates field-level validators (e.g., enforcing uppercase names) and model-level validators (e.g., receipt line items summing to total cost). Error messages from validators are conditionally added to the LLM prompt, enabling self-correction on retry. He notes validation errors are critical for observability and can fix most issues.

sections.title: RAG and Generation with Structured Outputs
sections.summary: Structured outputs enable follow-up question generation, URL validation via regex and HTTP POST to prevent hallucinated links, and sophisticated RAG with multi-index search. A search model with query, date ranges, limits, and source selection allows parallel queries for comparison questions. This yields an advanced RAG application in just two functions and two models.

sections.title: Data Extraction
sections.summary: Jason shows classification with Literal types (spam/not spam), with chain-of-thought improving accuracy by ~15%. He demonstrates transcript extraction producing structured output with meeting type, title, action items, and summary, noting that owner fields could be validated against participant lists.

sections.title: Advanced Types, Year-One Learnings, and Conclusions
sections.summary: Jason demonstrates advanced PEP type annotations for extracting tables from images, using custom validators and serializers that enable IDE autocomplete for data frame methods while serializing to markdown for the LLM. He shares year-one learnings: one retry suffices for OpenAI/Anthropic, informative error messages are essential, faster models make latency costs acceptable, and fine-tuning on function calling reduces 4-5% complex validation failure rates to zero even for simple models. He argues structured outputs are here to stay across vision, RAG, and agents, with enterprise RAG moving toward report generation and agents toward generating workflows and DAGs for execution engines rather than react loops. He concludes there are no new abstractions—just reducing LLMs to classical programming with types, turning generative AI into generating data structures, making software 3.0 backward compatible with existing software.
